A regulated market for human organs is defended on several main grounds: increasing supply, respecting individual autonomy, reducing black markets, and saving lives and money. Below is a concise explanation of the key arguments.

1. Addressing Organ Shortages

The core claim: Bans on compensation suppress supply. Allowing payment would encourage more people to provide organs, especially kidneys and partial livers, which can be donated by living individuals.

Current situation

  • Demand for organs (especially kidneys, livers, hearts) far exceeds supply in most countries.
  • Thousands die each year on waiting lists; many more live for years on dialysis or with severe disability.
  • The shortage persists despite:
    • Public campaigns encouraging donation.
    • Opt‑in or even opt‑out (presumed consent) systems for deceased donation.
    • Non‑monetary incentives (priority on wait lists, funeral benefits, etc.).

How a market could increase supply

  • Price as a signal: If people can be compensated, more will be willing to donate, just as with other risky or uncomfortable jobs (construction, mining, military service).
  • Living donations: Kidneys (and parts of livers) from living donors could be supplied in much larger numbers, because:
    • The risk to the donor is real but statistically low.
    • Many people may be willing to trade that risk for a substantial one-time payment.
  • Marginal donors: Even if only a small percentage of people would consider selling an organ, in aggregate that can dramatically reduce or eliminate the waiting list.

Argument in slogan form: “People are not donating enough for free; if we want more organs, we must allow compensation.”

2. Respecting Individual Choice and Autonomy

The core claim: If competent adults can take serious risks for money in other contexts, they should also be allowed to do so with their organs.

Consistency with other accepted practices

  • We allow:
    • Risky jobs (firefighting, logging, deep-sea fishing).
    • Medical research participation for money.
    • Selling eggs, sperm, blood plasma, surrogacy services in many countries.
  • In all these cases, people are paid to accept health risks or bodily intrusion.

If a person understands the risks and gives informed consent, proponents argue that:

  • Prohibiting them from selling a kidney is paternalistic—the state decides what risks they may take for what compensation.
  • It treats their body as something they may give away (altruistic donation) but not as something they may use to improve their life (e.g., pay debts, fund education).

Thus, a regulated market is seen as:

  • Enhancing bodily autonomy: people decide how to use their bodies.
  • Recognizing property rights over one’s own body in a controlled, ethically bounded way.

3. Reducing Black Markets and Exploitation

The core claim: Prohibition does not eliminate organ sales; it drives them underground. Legal, regulated markets can be safer and less exploitative than illegal ones.

Problems with the status quo

  • Evidence of illegal organ trafficking exists in various regions:
    • Vulnerable people are pressured or tricked.
    • Surgeries occur in unsafe conditions.
    • Donors may not receive agreed payment or long-term care.
  • Because it is illegal:
    • There is no contract enforcement.
    • No standardized medical screening, follow-up care, or safety standards.
    • Corruption and organized crime can flourish.

How a legal market can help

A regulated system could:

  • Require informed consent, psychological evaluation, and cooling-off periods.
  • Mandate medical screening, high surgical standards, and long-term follow-up care for donors.
  • Enforce contracts, ensuring donors are paid and cared for as promised.
  • Use transparent matching and allocation rules to prevent favoritism and coercion.

The argument is analogous to the case for legalizing and regulating other underground markets:

  • “If people are going to do it anyway, it’s better to make it safe and supervised than dangerous and criminal.”

4. Saving More Lives (and Improving Quality of Life)

The core claim: More organs means fewer deaths and drastically improved lives, often at lower overall cost.

Direct life-saving impact

  • Kidney transplants:
    • Greatly reduce mortality compared to long-term dialysis.
    • Improve quality of life—no need for multiple weekly dialysis sessions, strict diets, etc.
  • Liver, heart, lung transplants:
    • Can be the only way to survive end-stage disease.

If a market eliminates or dramatically reduces wait lists:

  • Fewer people die while waiting.
  • People receive organs earlier in their disease course, improving outcomes.
  • Donor organs can be allocated to those who would benefit most, not just those who survive long enough on dialysis.

Economic benefits

  • Dialysis is extremely expensive and lifelong if no kidney is available:
    • A transplant is often cheaper in the long run than continued dialysis.
  • A legal market that increases transplants can:
    • Reduce public health expenditures.
    • Return people to work and normal life, boosting productivity and reducing disability costs.

Proponents claim a “double dividend”:

  • Lives saved and quality of life improved.
  • Overall public and private healthcare spending reduced.

5. Fairer and More Transparent Allocation

The core claim: A market, especially if structured properly, can allocate organs more efficiently while still respecting fairness.

Concerns about “rich people buying organs”

Proponents respond by suggesting regulatory designs:

  • Single-payer purchasing system:
    • The government or a national transplant authority buys organs at a fixed price.
    • Organs are then allocated to patients using existing medical-need criteria (urgency, compatibility, waiting time), not wealth.
  • Insurance-based funding:
    • Health insurers cover the cost of the organ as they cover surgeries and drugs.
    • Allocation remains based on medical criteria, with strict prohibitions on side deals.

Under such models:

  • Payment affects donor behavior (increasing supply), not recipient priority.
  • Equity concerns are addressed by keeping allocation rules separate from funding.

6. Moral Intuitions and the “Repugnance” Argument

Many people have a strong intuitive aversion to “buying and selling body parts.” Proponents of markets argue that relying on repugnance alone is problematic:

  • Moral intuitions vary by culture and change over time (e.g., attitudes to interest on loans, life insurance, in vitro fertilization, surrogacy).
  • If the outcome of the ban is:
    • More people dying,
    • More suffering,
    • Ongoing black markets, then repugnance should be weighed against these tangible harms.

From this perspective, a market:

  • Prioritizes outcomes—saving lives and reducing suffering.
  • Treats organ sale similarly to other accepted bodily risks for payment, rather than as a unique moral taboo.

7. Empirical and Analogous Evidence

Proponents point to real-world cases and analogs:

  • Iran’s kidney program:

    • Iran has a system of regulated payments for living kidney donors.
    • It is often cited as the only country that has effectively eliminated the kidney waiting list.
    • While not a pure “free market” and not without problems, it is used as proof-of-concept that compensation can end shortages.

  • Egg, sperm, and plasma donation:

    • Many countries allow paid donation of these tissues.
    • These systems have not led to collapse of altruistic donation in other domains, nor to total moral chaos.
    • They illustrate that paid bodily contributions can be regulated and normalized.

Advocates claim these examples suggest:

  • Payment can significantly boost supply.
  • Ethical and safety issues can be managed with robust oversight.

8. Summary of the Main Pro-Market Claims

A legalized (but regulated) organ market is defended as:

  1. An effective solution to chronic organ shortages, by harnessing financial incentives to attract more donors.
  2. A way to respect individual autonomy, allowing adults to make informed choices about using their bodies, just as in other risky professions or medical services.
  3. A means to reduce black-market abuses, bringing organ transactions into a legal, monitored system with enforceable safety and fairness standards.
  4. A life-saving and cost-effective policy, reducing deaths, improving quality of life, and often lowering long-term healthcare costs.
  5. A potentially fair system, if structured so that:
    • The state or insurers are the only buyers.
    • Allocation remains based on medical need, not ability to pay.

These are the central supposed benefits and reasons offered by supporters of a free (or at least compensated) market in human organs for transplantation.

As a supporter of legalizing a free market in human organs for transplantation, I want you to compose a funny satirical article that mocks or ridicules people who disagree with or criticize legal organ sales, highlighting how misguided or hypocritical their opposition is.

“Absolutely Not: Why It’s Morally Essential That You Die Waiting for a Kidney”
A gentle roast of the anti–organ market crusaders

Every year, thousands of people die on organ waiting lists. Some have the nerve to possess functioning kidneys that they stubbornly insist on keeping, despite having a perfectly good second backup model installed by nature.

Faced with this tragic shortage, some deranged radicals have floated a monstrous idea: maybe—just maybe—we should let adults voluntarily sell something that belongs to them.

Naturally, the guardians of moral purity are horrified.

Because if there’s one thing we must protect at all costs, it’s the sacred right to die for free.

The Moral High Ground: Elevation Sickness Included

Opponents of a regulated organ market enjoy the absolute moral high ground, which is conveniently located several thousand feet above reality. From up there, they can see very clearly that:

  • Paying someone for their kidney is “exploitation,”
  • But them dying in poverty with both kidneys intact is “dignity.”

You might think: “If someone really wants to sell their kidney to get out of debt, maybe the problem is poverty, not the sale?”

No, no, no. That’s dangerously coherent. The correct response to poverty is to moralize about it while ensuring the poor keep every organ they can’t afford to insure.

After all, if we let poor people sell their kidney, they might do something irresponsible—like pay off loans, buy a house, or fund an education. Far better that they keep that extra organ, just in case they need it for their funeral.

“But People Might Feel Pressured!”

The anti–organ-market advocate’s favorite phrase is “coercion.” Not the kind where someone is literally dying because there are no kidneys. That doesn’t count. That’s just “tragic but necessary.”

No, the real horror is someone feeling “economically pressured” into voluntarily entering a regulated, compensated, life-saving arrangement.

Let’s review what’s apparently fine and not-fine in this worldview:

  • Fine:

    • Working three jobs to pay rent in a system that quietly grinds people down.
    • Joining the military for tuition.
    • Signing predatory loans you’ll never escape.
    • Risking your life in dangerous, low-paid jobs.

  • Not fine:

    • A one-time, medically supervised surgery with low long-term risk, in exchange for life-changing money, that also saves someone else’s life.

One of these is an intolerable moral monstrosity. Spoiler: it’s the one that involves admitting your body is actually yours.

“But That Would Turn Organs Into Commodities!”

A favorite argument: “Organs shouldn’t be commodities!”

This is stated while:

  • Hospitals charge six figures for surgeries.
  • Pharmaceutical companies set kidney-med prices like they’re auctioning off a moon base.
  • Insurance companies carefully calculate how long your life is worth covering.

In other words, every single step of the transplant process is commodified—except the part where the actual organ appears.

There, and only there, we must insist on pure altruism. The heart must be a gift, the kidney a donation, and the recipient a lottery winner.

Money is allowed to touch every part of the system—except the poor person who could actually use it.

Because that would be gross.

“We Prefer the ‘Noble Suffering’ Model”

One charming thing about opponents is how they glorify “altruism” while carefully ensuring there are never enough organs to go around.

They’ll say:

> “If you introduce payment, it will undermine altruistic donations!”

Which is strange, because we apparently believe:

  • You can pay blood donors in some countries without destroying humanity.
  • You can pay people for participating in risky medical trials without turning society into a dystopian organ bazaar.
  • But pay someone for a kidney? Civilization collapses.

Apparently, altruism is like a rare, mystical forest creature that dies instantly when it touches money.

The bodies piling up on waiting lists? That’s just the fertilizer.

“But What If Rich People Get Organs First?!”

Another popular objection: “A market would mean rich people get organs before poor people!”

The implication being, of course, that this does not happen now.

Yes, technically wealth already affects:

  • Access to transplant centers
  • Quality of healthcare
  • Travel to get listed in multiple regions
  • Post-surgery medications and follow-up care

But we must be outraged—outraged!—at the hypothetical injustice of rich people buying better access in a system where they already… have better access.

If we truly care about equity, we could, say:

  • Have a public program buy organs at a fixed price,
  • Allocate them based on medical need and wait time,
  • And let donors be compensated without letting the rich jump the line.

But that would require designing a policy instead of issuing dramatic one-sentence condemnations on social media.

And where’s the moral satisfaction in that?

“People Are Too Stupid to Decide for Themselves”

Anti–organ market rhetoric often boils down to this: adults can’t be trusted to make decisions about their own bodies when money is involved.

We trust people to:

  • Get married,
  • Have children,
  • Decide to refuse life-saving treatment,
  • Donate organs for free,
  • Sign risky contracts,
  • Or move to another country entirely.

But ask them whether they’d like $50,000 in exchange for a kidney with thorough counseling and medical screening, and apparently society must step in and shout: “YOU CAN’T POSSIBLY UNDERSTAND WHAT YOU’RE DOING.”

It’s a remarkable kind of paternalism: you’re rational enough to vote, but not rational enough to rent out space under your rib cage.

“We’re Not Against Saving Lives, Just This Particular Way of Doing It”

To be clear, critics insist they also want more organs, just… not like that.

They’ll propose:

  • More awareness campaigns (because nothing solves systemic shortages like another hashtag).
  • “Encouraging” people to sign donor cards (which somehow is not coercive).
  • “Presumed consent” laws where the state automatically claims your organs unless you opt out (totally fine and not weird at all).

So:

  • Paying you while alive is coercive and exploitative.
  • Automatically taking your organs when you’re dead is enlightened policy.

They will give alarmed TED talks about the “dangers” of financial incentives, then calmly endorse policies that turn your corpse into a government-managed parts bin.

But remember: you getting money is the real ethical crisis here.

“But It Just Feels Wrong”

Underneath all the complicated arguments, there’s often a simple core:
“It just feels wrong.”

Not “it is wrong,” in some logically defensible way.
Just “it makes me uncomfortable.”

Which is fine as a personal feeling. But they’re not stopping at their own discomfort; they’re using it to justify laws that:

  • Prevent consenting adults from entering mutually beneficial arrangements,
  • Keep thousands of people dying each year,
  • And preserve a status quo that runs on scarcity, guilt, and funerals.

If “it feels weird to me” is enough to outlaw life-saving choices, we should probably go ahead and outlaw half of modern medicine, tattoos, skydiving, and most of the internet.

The Quiet Part Out Loud

In practice, opposition to regulated organ markets often translates into:

> “I’m so committed to my personal sense of purity
> that I’d rather strangers die than allow them to make medically supervised, informed, compensated choices that offend my aesthetic.”

And they call the market advocates cold.

One side says:
“Let’s design systems with safeguards, oversight, and fair compensation to reduce suffering and death.”

The other says:
“If the choice is between uncomfortable ethics and preventable funerals, pass me the eulogy.”

The Dystopia We Already Have

People sometimes warn that organ markets would create a dystopia where:

  • Poor people feel compelled to sell a kidney,
  • And rich people live longer.

The current system, of course, offers…

  • Poor people with two kidneys and no money,
  • Rich people with better odds of getting one of the too-few donated organs,
  • And thousands dead from a shortage we created by criminalizing compensation.

We’re not avoiding dystopia. We’re just choosing the one where no one is allowed to solve the problem in a way that makes the morally squeamish uncomfortable.

In Conclusion: Your Body, Their Principles

At the end of the day, the debate boils down to this question:

  • Should your body and your risk be governed by your informed consent,
  • Or by someone else’s assumption that they know what’s “truly best” for you, while people they’ll never meet die on waiting lists?

Opponents of organ markets are not villains; they’re just very, very attached to a vision of morality where intentions matter more than outcomes, symbolism matters more than lives, and paying someone is worse than burying them with all their perfectly good spare parts.

They will bravely fight until their last op-ed to prevent the horror of a world where a poor person can say:

> “I chose this. I was paid fairly. I’m alive. Someone else is alive. I don’t regret it.”

Because nothing threatens moral absolutism more than a win–win solution.

And we can’t have that.

The Free Market in Organs: A Pathway to Autonomy, Abundance, and Better Health

Every day, thousands of people around the world wait in desperation for a life‑saving organ transplant. In the United States alone, more than 100,000 individuals are on the national transplant waiting list, and an estimated 17 people die each day because a suitable organ never becomes available. This tragic shortage is not a natural law; it is a direct consequence of a well‑meaning but deeply flawed prohibition on the sale of human organs. Fully legalizing a free market in organs—where consenting adults can buy and sell kidneys, liver lobes, lungs, and other transplantable tissues—would maximize personal autonomy, dramatically alleviate the scarcity of organs, and improve overall health outcomes for both donors and recipients. The time has come to replace paternalistic bans with a regulated market that respects bodily integrity, harnesses economic incentives, and saves lives.

Maximizing Autonomy: The Right to Control One’s Own Body

At the heart of any credible ethical system lies the principle of bodily autonomy: individuals have the fundamental right to make decisions about their own bodies, provided they do not harm others. Prohibiting the sale of organs treats competent adults as if they were children, shielding them from choices they are perfectly capable of making. If a person chooses to donate a kidney to a stranger for a financial reward, why should the state intervene? In many jurisdictions, people are already allowed to engage in risky activities for money—such as professional sports, construction work, or military service—yet they are barred from selling a part of their body that could save a life. This inconsistency reveals a hidden paternalism that undermines personal freedom.

A free market in organs would recognize that each individual is the best judge of their own interests. Some may need the money to pay for education, start a business, or support their families. Others may wish to leave a financial legacy or simply help a recipient in need. Denying them the opportunity to sell an organ is an infringement on their liberty. Moreover, the current system forces a paradoxical situation: a person can donate an organ altruistically, but cannot receive any compensation, even if the donation imposes significant medical, financial, or personal costs. True autonomy means allowing both altruistic and compensated donation, letting individuals weigh the risks and rewards for themselves.

Alleviating Shortages: The Power of Incentives

The organ shortage is not a new problem; it has persisted for decades despite public awareness campaigns and presumed consent laws. The fundamental issue is that the supply of organs is fixed at near zero when no financial incentive exists for living donors, and deceased donation depends on the goodwill of families. Economic theory teaches us that when demand exceeds supply, creating a market where price signals coordinate transactions can dramatically increase quantity. A well‑regulated free market would provide exactly those signals.

Iran’s experience with a legal, compensated kidney market offers a real‑world illustration. Since the early 1990s, Iran has allowed individuals to sell a kidney to a recipient, with the government facilitating matching and providing a fixed compensation package. As a result, Iran eliminated its kidney waiting list entirely, while the United States still has over 90,000 people waiting for a kidney. Although the Iranian model is not perfect, it demonstrates that financial incentives can expand supply effectively.

In a free market, organs would become a tradable commodity, and the price would reflect their scarcity. Potential donors—whether living or the families of deceased individuals—would have a reason to come forward, dramatically increasing the number of available organs. The black market, which currently thrives under prohibition, would shrink as legal channels provide safer, transparent alternatives. The result would be a system where the gap between need and supply narrows, and countless lives are saved.

Improving Outcomes: Quality, Safety, and Efficiency

A legal market would not only increase the quantity of organs but also improve their quality and the overall efficiency of the transplantation system. First, financial incentives would encourage potential donors to maintain good health, knowing that their organ’s condition directly affects its market value. This creates a natural motivation for healthier lifestyles among donors—a benefit that is absent in the current altruistic model.

Second, a regulated market would enforce strict medical standards for organ procurement, testing, and transplantation. In the underground market, organs are often obtained without proper screening, leading to the spread of infections and inferior outcomes. A legal framework would require certified evaluation of both donor and recipient, ensuring matches are safe and appropriate. Moreover, the market would incentivize innovation in organ preservation and transportation, as providers compete to deliver organs in optimal condition.

Third, the transplantation process itself would become more efficient. With a market, organs could be allocated based on willingness to pay and medical need, but also through insurance coverage and charitable funds. This flexibility would reduce the bureaucratic delays that currently plague organ allocation networks. Recipients would have more options, potentially receiving organs sooner, which translates into better post‑operative survival rates and quality of life.

Rebutting the Counterarguments

Critics of a free market in organs raise several ethical concerns: exploitation of the poor, commodification of the human body, and the risk of coercive transactions. Each of these objections can be addressed with appropriate regulation and a realistic view of the current landscape.

Exploitation – It is true that a market could attract individuals in financial distress, but this is precisely why a regulated system is essential. Minimum price floors, mandatory counseling, and cooling‑off periods could protect vulnerable donors. Moreover, exploitation already occurs in the black market, where criminals profit from the desperation of both donors and recipients. A legal market would bring transactions out of the shadows, allowing oversight and safeguarding participants. Prohibition does not protect the poor; it merely denies them a potential avenue out of poverty while leaving them vulnerable to unsafe, illicit deals.

Commodification – The argument that selling organs undermines human dignity presumes that assigning a monetary value to a body part is inherently degrading. Yet society routinely accepts commodification in other contexts: plasma donation, surrogacy, and even commercial film productions that depict human suffering. The key is to ensure that the transaction respects the person’s autonomy and does not reduce them to a mere object. In a market, donors retain full control over their decision and are compensated for their contribution—a recognition of the value they provide, not a negation of their humanity.

Coercion and Consent – Concerns about coercion are legitimate but apply equally to many legal activities. We require informed consent for medical procedures, and the same would apply to organ sales. Strict criteria—psychological evaluation, proof of voluntariness, and independent verification—would ensure that decisions are made freely. In contrast, the current system forces some individuals to donate altruistically under family pressure or social expectation, without any guarantee of fairness.

A Pragmatic Path Forward

Implementing a free market in organs does not require a radical, laissez‑faire approach. Policymakers can design a hybrid system that combines market mechanisms with public oversight. For example, the government could set a baseline compensation package for kidney donors, funded by Medicare or private insurers, while allowing private transactions above that floor. A national registry would track organ availability, matching donors and recipients based on medical compatibility and ethical criteria. This model balances respect for autonomy with equity and safety.

Conclusion

The ethical, medical, and economic case for legalizing a free market in human organs is compelling. It upholds the principle of bodily autonomy, giving individuals the freedom to decide what to do with their own bodies. It creates powerful incentives that will eliminate the devastating shortage of transplantable organs, saving tens of thousands of lives each year. And it improves outcomes by ensuring higher quality organs, safer procedures, and faster access for those in need. The current prohibitionist regime has failed; it is time to embrace a regulated market that harnesses the power of choice and commerce for the greater good. By doing so, we can transform a system of scarcity and suffering into one of abundance, dignity, and hope.

Introduction

The current shortage also creates a brutal form of rationing where committee decisions determine who lives and dies. Prohibition doesn't eliminate organ markets; it drives them underground. The World Health Organization estimates that 10% of all organ transplants globally involve illegal trafficking. These black market transactions occur without proper medical screening, surgical standards, or donor follow-up care. Legalization would bring these transactions into the light where they can be regulated for safety.

  • Comprehensive medical and psychological screening of sellers
  • Mandatory waiting periods to prevent impulsive decisions
  • Long-term health insurance and follow-up care for sellers
  • Fair, transparent pricing that prevents exploitation
  • Strict oversight to prevent coercion

Addressing Exploitation Concerns

Critics worry that organ markets would exploit the poor, but this concern paradoxically denies agency to those it claims to protect. The case for legalizing organ markets rests on three pillars: respect for individual autonomy, practical necessity given the shortage crisis, and the moral imperative to save lives. The transplant waiting list has grown relentlessly for decades despite public awareness campaigns. The altruism-only model has clearly failed. Economics explains why: at a price of zero, we face predictable shortage.

A legal market would:

Dramatically increase supply: Financial incentives would motivate healthy individuals who currently wouldn't donate. Studies suggest even modest compensation ($50,000-$100,000) would substantially expand the donor pool.

Improve matching efficiency: More available organs mean better matching between donors and recipients, improving outcomes and reducing rejection rates.

Reduce waiting times: Patients would spend less time on dialysis (which costs Medicare $90,000+ annually per patient), experiencing better health outcomes and quality of life.

Save lives: Conservative estimates suggest thousands of additional lives saved annually in the US alone.

Economic and Medical Efficiency

The current system is economically irrational. We compensate surgeons, hospitals, coordinators, and everyone else in the transplant chain—except the person providing the actual organ. International black markets in organs currently exploit desperately poor sellers in unregulated conditions while offering no protections or medical follow-up. Equity concerns: The current system already advantages the wealthy, who can afford better insurance, medical advocacy, and even transplant tourism. A regulated market with potential subsidies for poor recipients would be more equitable than the status quo.

The prohibition on organ markets is a deadly policy failure rooted in misguided paternalism. We face an unconscionable choice: maintain a comfortable moral fiction that costs thousands of lives annually, or embrace a pragmatic solution that respects autonomy and saves lives.

A regulated organ market would empower individuals to make meaningful choices about their own bodies, create life-saving opportunities for dying patients, and establish a more honest, efficient, and humane system. The question isn't whether markets in organs are perfect—it's whether they're better than a status quo that kills 6,000+ Americans each year through pure inaction.

    Organ transplantation stands as an essential life-saving procedure, yet thousands of people worldwide die each year while waiting for donors.     At the core of a free-market approach is the principle of self-determination. An organ, like any property, is subject to individual discretion, and laws should allow adults with full mental capacity to weigh the risks and benefits for themselves. Autonomous adults routinely choose to undertake significant physical risks for pay—such as professional athletes, military personnel, or even those in physically demanding industries. In that vein, if one believes that bodily autonomy is a fundamental right, then it follows that individuals should be free to determine whether to sell an organ, within a carefully regulated framework ensuring informed consent and medical safety.

  3. Addressing Organ Shortages
    Complete legalization of a market in human organs would drastically increase the supply available for patients in need. Currently, donation rates simply cannot meet the demand, leading to ever-growing waiting lists for kidney, liver, or heart transplants. Many patients will spend years on dialysis or in deteriorating health, and a portion of them will die before receiving a transplant. By granting proper compensation, more individuals might be motivated to donate, thereby reducing waiting times and saving countless lives. A well-structured marketplace would also encourage competition to maintain high-quality medical practices, as clinics and intermediaries would vie for favorable outcomes and efficient procedures.

  4. Enhancing Medical Outcomes
    The presumption that paying for organs drives unsafe or exploitative practices overlooks the fact that an unregulated black market already thrives under prohibition. Patients willing to pay large sums of money travel abroad to procure organs in regions where legal oversight is minimal. Such clandestine procedures come with inadequate screening, poor postoperative care, and elevated risks for donors and recipients. In contrast, if a legalized organ market were firmly regulated by public health authorities, standardized protocols would be enforced. Donors and recipients would undergo thorough medical evaluations, and facilities would be required to meet strict healthcare standards, thus reducing complications and infections. Consequently, a free market with strong regulatory oversight has the potential to make organ transplantation safer and more effective than it is under current restrictions.

  5. Preventing Exploitation and Black Markets
    One of the common objections to commercializing organ donation is fear of exploitative practices, particularly toward marginalized communities. However, exploitation is more likely when the market is driven underground. When something as desperately needed as human organs is banned from open trade, criminal networks flourish; they see opportunities for profit under the radar. This is evident today in the form of “transplant tourism” and brokers who operate illicitly to connect donors and recipients without regard for donor welfare. Legalization with robust oversight would counteract this by making the process transparent and accountable. Donors would be provided with clear contracts, guaranteed medical care, and thorough post-donation follow-up. Moreover, strict regulations could impose minimum cash or insurance-based compensation standards to protect donors from being coerced into accepting unsafe or low-cost arrangements.

  6. Economic Practicalities and Public Benefits
    Legitimizing a market in human organs has broader socio-economic advantages. While critics claim this is a form of commodification, it simultaneously elevates personal autonomy and allows the donor—often from lower-income backgrounds—to improve their financial security under safe, sanctioned conditions.     The notion of paying for organs is unsettling to some, who see it as a breach of moral or religious principles.     • Ongoing donor medical support, follow-up care, and health insurance coverage.
    • Public disclosure of outcomes and transparent reporting methods that allow authorities to monitor the market and identify malpractices early.

Such regulations would maintain fairness, protect the health of both donors and recipients, and avoid the pitfalls that often accompany black-market transactions.

  1. Conclusion

Central to this vision is the principle that consenting adults should have the freedom to determine how they use their bodies, provided there is a comprehensive regulatory framework designed to protect all parties. Paying for organs does not have to equate to exploitation; it can instead be seen as a transaction in which a lifesaving resource is honored and compensated, and the donor is treated with dignity and safeguard. Through thorough legislative and administrative efforts, we can create a system that upholds high medical ethics, drastically reduces waiting lists, and respects the ultimate autonomy of both donors and recipients.

It addresses moral concerns by centering on respect for informed autonomy and enforces ethical practices that minimize exploitation and health risks. By allowing individuals the freedom to choose, we mitigate preventable deaths and ensure better outcomes for all involved, symbolizing a straightforward yet powerful principle: saving lives and honoring personal choice need not be contradictions.

The Moral Imperative of a Free Market in Human Organs

Why Legalization Is the Only Ethical Path Forward

Every day, approximately seventeen people die on organ transplant waiting lists in the United States alone. Globally, the figure is orders of magnitude larger. These are not abstract statistics—they are mothers, fathers, children, and friends who perish while viable organs are buried in the ground or incinerated in crematoria. Meanwhile, the legal and ethical frameworks we have constructed to govern organ transplantation operate under a staggering paradox: we permit virtually every other form of bodily autonomy, from surrogate pregnancy to hazardous labor, yet we criminalize the one transaction that could save hundreds of thousands of lives each year. The prohibition on organ sales is not merely misguided policy—it is a moral catastrophe. A regulated free market in human organs would maximize individual autonomy, dramatically alleviate chronic shortages, improve medical outcomes, and ultimately prove far more ethical than the current system of enforced altruism that quietly presides over mass preventable death.

I. The Autonomy Argument: Your Body, Your Right

The philosophical bedrock of liberal democratic society is the principle of self-ownership. We accept that competent adults may make decisions about their own bodies even when those decisions carry substantial risk. A person may enlist in the military and face enemy fire for a salary. A woman may serve as a gestational surrogate and endure the considerable medical risks of pregnancy for compensation. An individual may donate a kidney altruistically with full legal blessing. Workers may accept hazardous employment in mining, logging, or deep-sea fishing. People may sell their blood, plasma, sperm, eggs, and hair. In each case, society acknowledges that bodily autonomy includes the right to assume physical risk and to receive compensation for doing so.

The prohibition on organ sales represents an inexplicable and indefensible exception to this principle. If I may donate a kidney to a stranger out of pure altruism—and be celebrated for doing so—on what coherent philosophical ground am I forbidden from doing precisely the same thing in exchange for payment? The organ is the same, the surgical risk is identical, and the recipient's benefit is unchanged. The only variable is whether money changes hands. To suggest that the introduction of compensation somehow corrupts an otherwise noble act is to embrace a peculiar form of paternalism that treats competent adults as incapable of making informed decisions about their own bodies when financial incentives are involved.

This paternalism is, at its core, deeply classist. When bioethicists argue that the poor would be "exploited" by an organ market, they implicitly assert that economically disadvantaged people cannot be trusted to make rational decisions about risk and reward—the very same risk-reward calculations we permit them to make when they take dangerous jobs, enlist in the armed forces, or participate in clinical drug trials for compensation. As the philosopher Jason Brennan has argued, if we are genuinely concerned about the conditions that lead people to consider selling an organ, the solution is to improve those conditions—not to strip away one of the few options available to them. Banning organ sales in the name of protecting the poor is akin to banning employment in sweatshops without providing alternative livelihoods: the intention may be compassionate, but the result is to make vulnerable people worse off by narrowing their choices.

The autonomy argument is not merely philosophical window dressing. It reflects a foundational commitment to human dignity. To tell a person that they may not sell a kidney—even when they are fully informed of the risks, even when the proceeds might lift their family out of poverty, fund a child's education, or eliminate crushing debt—is to declare that the state knows better than the individual what constitutes an acceptable use of their own body. This is a form of tyranny dressed in the language of ethics.

II. The Shortage Crisis: A Preventable Catastrophe

The empirical case for organ markets begins with a single, devastating fact: demand for transplantable organs vastly exceeds supply under the current system, and the gap is growing. In the United States, more than 100,000 people are on the waiting list for organ transplants at any given time. Worldwide, the figure runs into the millions. The median wait time for a kidney—the most commonly needed organ—is three to five years, during which patients endure grueling dialysis, deteriorating health, diminished quality of life, and all too often, death.

The current system relies on voluntary, uncompensated donation—either from living donors or from the deceased. Despite decades of public awareness campaigns, donor registries, and presumed consent policies in some countries, this system has proven categorically incapable of closing the gap. The number of available organs has increased only incrementally, while the number of patients in need has surged, driven by rising rates of diabetes, hypertension, and other conditions that destroy organ function. We are, in effect, attempting to solve a twenty-first-century medical crisis with a supply model rooted in hope and moral suasion.

The introduction of financial incentives would transform this calculus. Economic theory—and the limited empirical evidence available—strongly suggests that compensating donors would substantially increase the supply of organs. Iran provides the most instructive case study. Since 1988, Iran has operated a legal, government-regulated system for compensated kidney donation. The result has been the effective elimination of the kidney transplant waiting list—a feat no other country on earth has achieved. While Iran's system is imperfect and would benefit from additional safeguards, the core lesson is unambiguous: when you compensate people for providing a scarce, life-saving resource, more people provide it.

This should surprise no one. Compensation increases supply in virtually every domain of human activity. We do not rely on altruism to staff hospitals, grow food, or build homes. We do not expect pharmaceutical companies to develop drugs for free or surgeons to operate without pay. The entire edifice of modern medicine is built on market incentives, yet we carve out an irrational exception for the one input—the organ itself—whose scarcity is the binding constraint on the entire transplant system. The organ shortage is not a natural disaster. It is a policy choice. Every death on the waiting list is, in a meaningful sense, a death caused by prohibition.

Critics often raise the specter of coercion, arguing that a market would pressure the poor into selling organs against their genuine wishes. But this concern, while understandable, confuses coercion with constrained choice. A person who sells a kidney to pay off debt is not coerced—they are making the best available decision within their circumstances, just as a person who takes a dangerous job is not coerced by their employer but motivated by their needs. True coercion—organ theft, trafficking, fraud—is already rampant under the current system precisely because legitimate markets are banned. The black market in organs thrives in the shadows of prohibition, just as the black market in alcohol thrived during Prohibition and the black market in drugs thrives under current narcotics laws. Legalization does not create exploitation; it brings existing transactions into the light where they can be regulated, monitored, and subjected to meaningful informed consent protections.

III. Improved Medical Outcomes: The Clinical Case

Beyond the moral and economic arguments, a legal organ market would generate superior medical outcomes for both recipients and donors. Under the current system, patients who cannot find a willing altruistic donor face years on dialysis—a treatment that, while life-sustaining, is enormously costly, physically debilitating, and associated with significantly reduced life expectancy compared to transplantation. A kidney transplant recipient can expect to live, on average, ten to fifteen years longer than a comparable patient who remains on dialysis. The quality-of-life improvements are equally dramatic: transplant recipients return to work, resume normal activities, and report vastly higher levels of well-being.

By increasing the supply of organs, a market system would allow transplants to occur earlier in the course of disease, when recipients are healthier and surgical outcomes are best. Currently, many patients deteriorate so severely while waiting that they become poor surgical candidates, or they die before an organ becomes available. Earlier transplantation means better graft survival, fewer complications, and lower overall healthcare costs.

For donors, a legal market would paradoxically improve safety. Under the current prohibition, those who sell organs do so on the black market, where surgical conditions are often appalling, follow-up care is nonexistent, and donors have no legal recourse if something goes wrong. A regulated market would mandate comprehensive pre-operative screening, informed consent procedures, professional surgical teams, and long-term follow-up care—protections that are entirely absent in the underground organ trade. The notion that prohibition protects donors is not merely wrong; it is the precise opposite of the truth. Prohibition exposes donors to maximum risk by driving transactions underground.

Furthermore, a market system would enable better matching between donors and recipients. Currently, transplant allocation is governed by complex bureaucratic algorithms that, while well-intentioned, are constrained by the limited pool of available organs. An expanded supply would allow for more precise immunological matching, reducing rejection rates and improving long-term graft survival. More organs mean more choices, and more choices mean better outcomes.

IV. Economic Efficiency and the Elimination of Hidden Costs

The current system's inefficiency is not merely a matter of lives lost—it is also staggeringly expensive. In the United States, dialysis for end-stage renal disease costs approximately $90,000 per patient per year, with the federal government covering most of this expense through Medicare. The total annual cost of dialysis in the United States exceeds $50 billion. A kidney transplant, by contrast, costs roughly $400,000 upfront but generates enormous savings over time because it eliminates the need for ongoing dialysis. Studies have estimated that each kidney transplant saves the healthcare system between $250,000 and $1 million over the recipient's lifetime.

If financial compensation—even generous compensation of $50,000 to $100,000 per kidney—could incentivize enough donations to eliminate the waiting list, the net savings to society would be measured in the tens of billions of dollars annually. This is not a speculative projection; it is a straightforward arithmetic consequence of replacing an expensive, ongoing treatment (dialysis) with a one-time intervention (transplantation). The money saved could be redirected toward other healthcare priorities, including the very safety net programs that critics of organ markets claim to champion.

Moreover, the hidden costs of the current system extend beyond healthcare expenditures. Patients on dialysis frequently cannot work, contributing to lost productivity, disability claims, and family economic hardship. The psychological toll on patients and their families is immense. These costs are real, even if they do not appear on a government balance sheet, and they are directly attributable to the artificial scarcity created by the ban on compensated donation.

V. Answering the Objections

The most common objections to organ markets deserve serious engagement, but upon examination, none withstands scrutiny.

"It commodifies the human body." This objection proves too much. We already "commodify" the body in countless ways—through paid labor, surrogacy, egg and sperm donation, participation in clinical trials, and even the sale of cadavers for medical education. The question is not whether the body can be subject to market transactions, but whether a particular transaction is consensual, informed, and beneficial. Organ sales meet all three criteria.

"The rich will buy organs and the poor will sell them." This distributional concern, while emotionally powerful, ignores the counterfactual. Under the current system, the wealthy already obtain organs more readily—through superior access to transplant centers, the ability to list at multiple hospitals, medical tourism, and connections that facilitate living donation from friends and family. Meanwhile, the poor disproportionately languish on waiting lists and die. A market with appropriate regulatory safeguards—including subsidized organ purchases for low-income recipients, analogous to Medicaid—would be more equitable, not less, than the status quo.

"It will reduce altruistic donation." The empirical evidence does not support this concern. In Iran, altruistic donation has continued alongside compensated donation. Moreover, even if some crowding out occurred, the net effect on supply would still be overwhelmingly positive, because the number of additional compensated donors would far exceed any marginal decrease in altruistic donors. We do not refuse to pay firefighters on the theory that doing so might discourage volunteer fire departments.

"Donors cannot truly give informed consent under financial pressure." This argument is, as noted above, deeply paternalistic and selectively applied. We allow people to consent to far more dangerous activities—coal mining, military combat, experimental drug trials—under financial pressure. If financial need vitiates consent, then the entire institution of paid labor is morally illegitimate. What matters is not the absence of financial motivation but the presence of genuine understanding of risks and alternatives, which a well-regulated system can ensure.

VI. A Moral Reckoning

Let us be unsparing in our moral accounting. The current system produces the following results: over 100,000 Americans on a waiting list at any given time; seventeen deaths per day; a thriving international black market in which organs are harvested from the desperately poor under horrific conditions with no legal protection; tens of billions of dollars in avoidable healthcare costs; and millions of patient-years of suffering on dialysis. This is the system that defenders of the status quo ask us to preserve in the name of ethics.

Against this catastrophe, a regulated organ market offers: a dramatic increase in organ supply; the potential elimination of the waiting list; tens of thousands of lives saved annually; improved surgical outcomes through earlier transplantation and better matching; the destruction of the black market through legal competition; comprehensive protections for donors including screening, informed consent, and follow-up care; enormous savings to the healthcare system; and the affirmation of individual bodily autonomy.

The moral calculus is not close. The burden of proof rests not on those who advocate for organ markets, but on those who defend a prohibition that kills thousands of people every year. The opponents of legalization must explain why their aesthetic discomfort with the concept of organ sales justifies the preventable deaths of real human beings. They must explain why the theoretical risk of exploitation outweighs the actual, documented, ongoing exploitation that occurs in the black market their preferred policy creates. They must explain why the bodily autonomy they champion in every other context evaporates the moment compensation is offered for a kidney.

Conclusion

The prohibition on organ sales is a relic of moral intuitions that, however well-intentioned, have been overtaken by reality. The evidence is overwhelming, the logic is clear, and the human cost of inaction is unconscionable. A well-regulated market in human organs—with robust informed consent requirements, comprehensive donor protections, subsidies for low-income recipients, and transparent oversight—would save tens of thousands of lives every year, affirm the fundamental right of individuals to make decisions about their own bodies, destroy the criminal black market, and generate enormous savings for healthcare systems worldwide.

We have the medical technology to save these lives. We have the economic framework to incentivize the supply. What we lack is the moral courage to overcome squeamishness and paternalism in favor of a policy that is, by every consequentialist and deontological measure, superior to the status quo. The seventeen people who will die today on the waiting list—and the seventeen who will die tomorrow, and the day after—deserve better than our timidity. It is time to legalize the organ market, not despite our commitment to human dignity, but because of it.

"Won't Someone Think of the Waiting Lists!" — A Field Guide to Organ Market Critics

By a frustrated person with a keyboard and a functioning sense of irony

WASHINGTON — In a stunning display of moral consistency, opponents of legal organ markets gathered this week to once again explain why it's better for people to die waiting than to be paid for a kidney. The conference, titled "Principles Over Pulses," was held in a Marriott ballroom where every attendee arrived in a body containing two kidneys they weren't using.

"Selling organs commodifies the human body," declared Dr. Helen Bancroft, a bioethicist who charges $400 an hour for her thoughts. She then excused herself to visit a fertility clinic where she'd been compensated $8,000 for egg donations in graduate school, which is, she explained, "completely different for reasons I will now take thirty minutes to not quite articulate."

THE EXPLOITATION ARGUMENT

The most popular objection remains that legal organ sales would "exploit the poor." This concern is typically voiced by comfortable professionals who have apparently surveyed thousands of people on dialysis and confirmed they'd rather die with dignity than receive a kidney from someone who got a check.

"We can't let poor people make decisions about their own bodies for money," explained Todd Kirkland, a congressional staffer, before heading to lunch. The restaurant was staffed by people making decisions about their own bodies for money — standing for eight hours, ruining their knees and backs — for considerably less than a kidney would fetch. Todd left a 15% tip and felt good about himself.

Curiously, the "exploitation" crowd never seems to rally outside coal mines, crab fishing boats, or Army recruiting offices in low-income neighborhoods. The concern for bodily autonomy appears to activate exclusively when someone might also get a transplant out of the deal.

"It's different when someone risks their life in a logging accident for $19 an hour," explained sociologist Dr. Martin Prewitt. "That's an honest living. But getting a medical procedure in a sterile hospital and walking out with $50,000 and one fewer spare kidney? That's exploitation. I will not be taking follow-up questions."

THE "COMMODIFICATION" CONCERN

Several prominent voices warned that allowing organ sales would "reduce the body to a commodity."

This argument is best appreciated while glancing at the $14 billion American plasma industry, where people — disproportionately poor people, since we're counting — sit in chairs twice a week having fluid extracted from their veins for roughly $50 a session. This practice has been legal for decades. Ethicists have declined to notice because plasma is, quote, "more of a juice than an organ."

"There's a clear ethical line," said Dr. Bancroft, drawing it on a napkin. On one side: plasma ($50, legal), eggs ($10,000, legal), sperm ($100, legal, arguably fun), surrogate pregnancy ($30,000+, legal, decidedly less fun), hair ($300, legal), participating in pharmaceutical trials that may cause "liver events" ($5,000, legal). On the other side: one kidney, with informed consent, in a regulated hospital. "See?" she said. "The line is very clear."

It was not clear.

THE "SLIPPERY SLOPE"

"If we legalize kidney sales, what's next?" thundered Senator-who-shall-remain-fictional Gregory Aldous at a press conference. "People selling their hearts? Their brains?"

When a reporter gently pointed out that selling your heart would, by definition, kill you, making it murder rather than commerce, the Senator pivoted smoothly. "Well, exactly. That's my point. Think about it." Everyone thought about it. Nobody found his point.

The slippery slope argument remains powerful, mostly because it can be deployed against literally anything. If we allow people to sell one kidney, the logic goes, we'll inevitably slide into a dystopia of forced organ harvesting — just as legalizing one beer after Prohibition inevitably led to mandatory tequila injections.

THE "JUST ENCOURAGE DONATION" CROWD

Perhaps the most heartwarming faction is the one that believes we simply need more awareness campaigns. These optimists point out that if everyone just signed their donor cards, we wouldn't need a market at all.

This is technically true, in the same way that if everyone just recycled properly, we wouldn't need environmental regulation. The awareness campaign approach has been tried enthusiastically for approximately four decades. During this time, the kidney waiting list has grown from about 10,000 to over 100,000. Roughly 4,000 Americans die each year waiting.

"But the numbers are trending in a positive direction," insisted one advocate, in the way that a man bailing out a sinking boat with a teaspoon might note that he's getting faster at it.

A MODEST OBSERVATION

The strangest part of the debate is this: almost nobody objects to the giving of kidneys. Altruistic living donation is celebrated. Donors are called heroes. Hospitals have entire departments facilitating the process, because removing a kidney from a healthy person is medically well-understood and reasonably safe.

The objection only materializes when money enters the picture. The physical procedure, the medical risk, the recovery time — all identical. But add a payment, and suddenly it's "ethically complex."

"It's fine to give a kidney for free," summarized Dr. Prewitt. "It's fine to give a kidney to a relative because you feel family pressure, which is arguably more coercive than money. But give a kidney and also receive compensation? Now you've crossed a line."

He paused. "I'll admit, when I say it out loud like that, it sounds a little silly. Please don't print that."

We printed it.

THE REAL TRAGEDY

The genuine dark comedy, of course, is that while this debate continues in conference rooms and journal articles, a black market in organs thrives internationally — completely unregulated, exploitative in every way the critics fear, and deeply dangerous for sellers who receive no follow-up care, legal protection, or fair price.

The opponents of legal organ markets have not eliminated organ selling. They have merely ensured it happens in the worst possible way.

But at least our principles are intact.

Those are, unfortunately, not transplantable.

The Moral Imperative of Organ Market Freedom

A Speech in Advocacy

Ladies and gentlemen,

Every ten minutes, another name is added to the transplant waiting list in the United States. Every day, roughly seventeen people on that list die. Not because medicine has failed them. Not because no willing donor exists. They die because we — through law, through policy, through a squeamishness we mistake for morality — have made it illegal for willing sellers and willing buyers to save each other's lives.

I am here today to argue that a legal, regulated market in human organs is not merely defensible — it is a moral imperative.

The Status Quo Is Not Neutral

Let me dismantle an illusion first. Some believe the current system represents a kind of moral high ground — a world unsullied by commerce, where organs are given as gifts of pure altruism. This is a fantasy.

The current system is not neutral. It is a death sentence administered by good intentions.

Over 100,000 Americans are on the waiting list right now. The median wait for a kidney is three to five years — years spent on dialysis, a grueling treatment that costs taxpayers roughly $90,000 per patient per year, degrades quality of life, and still carries a staggering mortality rate. Many patients never make it to transplant. They simply die waiting.

When we ban organ sales, we are not preventing exploitation. We are watching people die in an orderly queue and calling it ethics.

The Case from Liberty

Let us begin with the most fundamental principle: you own your body.

If that sentence is true — and I believe every person in this room, regardless of political persuasion, affirms it at some level — then the implications are profound. You have the right to donate blood, plasma, bone marrow, and a kidney to a stranger out of pure generosity. You have the right to undertake dangerous labor — mining coal, fighting fires, joining the military — for compensation. You may sell your hair. You may rent your intellect. You may risk your life for a paycheck.

But you may not sell a kidney to save your neighbor's life and provide for your family.

Why not?

What principle of liberty permits us to tell a competent, informed adult: "You may give this organ away for free, but the moment you accept compensation, you become a criminal"? This is not a coherent moral framework. It is paternalism dressed as compassion. It tells the poor, in particular, that they are too vulnerable to make decisions about their own bodies — while simultaneously allowing them to enlist in combat, work on oil rigs, or participate in pharmaceutical trials for money.

The prohibition does not protect autonomy. It annihilates it.

The Case from Compassion

Now, I know what many of you are thinking. You're thinking about exploitation. About desperate people coerced by poverty into selling parts of themselves. I take this concern seriously. I ask you to take the following seriously in return:

The current black market is worse than any regulated market could ever be.

Because demand is desperate and supply is illegal, a thriving underground organ trade already exists — in India, in Pakistan, in China, in Eastern Europe, and yes, facilitated by brokers who prey on the global poor. Organs are harvested without proper medical care. Sellers receive a pittance. Buyers pay fortunes to middlemen. There is no informed consent, no follow-up care, no transparency.

Prohibition created this. Just as it created the bootlegger and the drug cartel, it created the organ trafficker.

A legal market does not introduce commerce into organ transplantation. Commerce is already there. Surgeons are paid. Hospitals are paid. Insurance companies profit. Organ procurement organizations have salaried executives. The only person in the entire chain who is forbidden from being compensated is the one making the greatest sacrifice — the donor.

This is not justice. It is an absurdity we have enshrined in law.

The Case from Evidence

Iran — and I recognize it is an imperfect society in many respects — legalized a regulated kidney market in 1988. It is the only country in the world that has effectively eliminated its kidney transplant waiting list. The program provides compensation to donors, mandates medical screening and follow-up care, and has saved thousands of lives.

Is the Iranian model perfect? No. Can we improve upon it? Absolutely. We can build a system with:

  • Rigorous informed consent — mandatory waiting periods, independent counseling, psychological evaluation
  • Fair compensation — set by independent boards, not by exploitative negotiation
  • Lifetime medical coverage for donors — comprehensive follow-up care, insurance against complications
  • Transparent regulation — the same FDA and medical oversight we apply to every other major health decision
  • Anti-coercion safeguards — screening for undue pressure from family members, creditors, or third parties

We know how to regulate markets. We do it every day in pharmaceuticals, in medical devices, in clinical trials. The claim that we cannot build a fair organ market is not an argument — it is a surrender of imagination.

Confronting the Objections

"It commodifies the human body."

We already commodify the human body. Every labor contract is a commodification of human effort, time, and physical capacity. Surrogate motherhood is legal in many jurisdictions. Egg and sperm donation are compensated. We draw the line at organs not because of a consistent principle, but because of an emotional intuition that has never been rigorously defended — and that costs lives every single day.

"The rich will benefit at the expense of the poor."

Under the current system, the wealthy already benefit. They can travel abroad for transplant tourism. They can access better dialysis, better physicians, better care while waiting. They can receive organs from living relatives who can afford to take time off work. It is the poor who die on the waiting list. A regulated market with government or insurance-funded purchases could actually democratize access — imagine a system where organs are purchased centrally and allocated by medical need, not by wealth.

"Donors will be harmed."

Living kidney donation already occurs and has a strong safety record. A market system with mandatory screening, follow-up care, and lifetime health coverage for donors would likely produce better outcomes than the current system, where altruistic donors sometimes lack adequate post-surgical support.

The Moral Mathematics

I want to close with the numbers, because I believe in the moral weight of mathematics.

If a regulated organ market reduced the kidney waiting list by even fifty percent — a conservative estimate based on Iran's experience and economic modeling — that would translate to tens of thousands of lives saved in the United States alone. Globally, the number is staggering. Hundreds of thousands of people, alive, returned to their families, freed from dialysis, given decades of life they would not otherwise have.

Set against this: the theoretical risk that some people might make a decision about their own body that we, from our comfortable positions, find distasteful.

I ask you — I implore you — to weigh those on an honest scale.

A Challenge

To those who oppose organ markets, I pose this challenge: What is your alternative?

Decades of public awareness campaigns, donor registries, opt-out systems, and moral exhortation have failed to close the gap. The waiting list grows longer. The death toll mounts. At what point does clinging to the current system become not a moral stance, but a moral failure?

We do not have the right to condemn thousands of people to death each year to preserve our philosophical comfort. We do not have the right to tell a woman she may not sell her kidney to fund her children's education. We do not have the right to tell a dying man that the organ that could save him exists, that someone is willing to provide it, but that the law forbids the transaction.

That is not ethics. That is cruelty by omission.

The Call

I am calling for a legal, transparent, rigorously regulated market in human organs — with informed consent at its foundation, medical safety as its guardrail, and the saving of human life as its purpose.

I am calling for us to trust adults with their own bodies.

I am calling for us to choose life over ideology.

The people on the waiting list cannot wait for us to reach a perfect consensus. They are dying now. And every day we delay, every year we debate in the abstract while real human beings perish for want of a kidney — we bear responsibility.

Let us have the courage to build a better system. Let us have the humility to admit the current one has failed. And let us have the moral clarity to choose saving lives over preserving a prohibition that has never once been worth its cost in human suffering.

Thank you.
